opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it really comes from what we've seen working with teams over the years. Annotation is never one-size-fits-all. Every team has its own ontology, its own quality checks, its own little quirks in how they want labels reviewed or corrected. And historically, the pattern has been: you export your data out of wherever it lives, you ship it to some annotation tool, you wait, you pull it back in, and then you discover the problems. That round trip is where so much time and so much signal gets lost.

What panels let us do in FiftyOne is bring that workflow right into the place where you're already looking at your data. A panel is essentially a customizable piece of the app. You can write it in Python, it's backed by the plugin framework, and it sits alongside your samples, your embeddings view, your model predictions. So if your team needs a particular review interface, say flagging label disagreements between two models, or a quick-fix tool for bounding boxes on a specific class, or a triage queue that prioritizes the samples your model is most uncertain about, you can build that as a panel and it lives right next to everything else.

The reason I see it as the way forward is really twofold. First, it keeps the human in the loop at the point of maximum context. When you're correcting a label, you want to see the embedding neighborhood, the model's confidence, the related samples, and panels give you that for free. Second, it's extensible without us having to anticipate every use case. We're never going to build the perfect annotation tool for every domain, whether it's autonomous driving, medical imaging, or agriculture. But we can build the substrate that lets the community and our customers build exactly what they need, and then share it.

Ultimately, I think annotation is moving away from being a big, separate, upfront labeling phase and toward something much more iterative and data-centric: look at your model's failures, fix the data that matters, retrain, repeat. Panels are how we make that loop tight and customizable inside a single environment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the context here is FiftyOne, which is the open-source tool we build at Voxel51 for visual data, and the thing I've come to believe pretty strongly is that annotation is never a one-size-fits-all problem. Every team I talk to has some wrinkle. Maybe they're labeling 3D point clouds alongside images, maybe they've got a medical use case with a very specific ontology, maybe they need a reviewer sign-off step baked into the loop. Historically, the way you handled that was you went and bought a labeling platform, and then you spent six months bending your workflow to fit that platform, or writing glue code to shuttle data back and forth between it and wherever your data actually lived.

Panels flip that around. A panel is basically a custom view inside the FiftyOne app, written in Python, that lives right next to your data. So instead of exporting a dataset to some external tool, labeling, re-importing, and hoping nothing broke in the round trip, you can build the annotation interface itself as a panel. You've got the samples, the metadata, the model predictions, the embeddings, all right there, and the panel can read and write to the dataset directly.

What I find exciting about that is it collapses the distance between the person looking at the data and the person building the tooling. A machine learning engineer who knows a bit of Python can stand up a specialized labeling flow in an afternoon. And because it's in the same environment where you're doing curation, where you're finding failure modes, where you're comparing model versions, annotation stops being this separate phase that happens somewhere else. It becomes part of the same iterative loop. You find the hard examples, you label them in place, you retrain, you look again.

The other piece is composability. Panels can talk to operators, which are our mechanism for running arbitrary compute, so you can wire in model-assisted labeling, active learning strategies, quality checks, whatever you want, without us having to anticipate every workflow. We're not trying to build the one true annotation tool. We're trying to give people the primitives so they can build the one that's right for them.

astra-6.text:
I think panels give you a way to bring the annotation workflow into the same environment where you’re already exploring your data. When you find an example that needs attention, you want to act on it right there, with the context that helped you identify the problem in the first place.

And annotation isn’t one uniform task. Different teams have different data, different labeling requirements, and different review processes. The idea with panels is to give them room to build the interaction that makes sense for their workflow, while keeping it connected to the dataset.

That makes the loop much tighter: you explore, identify an issue, annotate or correct it, and then look at what changed. To me, that’s the opportunity—making custom annotation part of an ongoing process of understanding and improving your data.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that annotation needs to be part of the loop of understanding and improving your data. You’re exploring a dataset, you find something that needs to be labeled or corrected, and you want to act on it right there.

Panels give you a way to bring that custom interaction into FiftyOne. The workflow can reflect your particular data, your task, and how your team works. Maybe you’re reviewing predictions, correcting labels, or selecting examples to send out for annotation. You can put the controls for those steps alongside the data you’re looking at.

That’s why I see them as a way forward: we can provide the foundation for visualizing and interacting with the data, and people can build the annotation workflow that makes sense for their problem.
